items.title: [phys.org] Global study finds glacial lakes speed ice loss; researcher urges safety oversight
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

A global analysis found that glaciers ending in lakes lost ice faster from 2000 to 2020 than glaciers ending on land or at sea, while a separate paper calls for formal safety oversight of hazardous glacial lakes. Lake-terminating glaciers lost an annual average of 0.66 meters of water equivalent, compared with 0.40 meters for land-terminating and 0.36 meters for marine-terminating glaciers. Ice-contact lakes explained an estimated 11% of mass loss among lake-terminating glaciers, compared with larger contributions from glacier geometry and climate. The study counted 3,567 more lakes in direct contact with glaciers in 2020 than in 2000, a 35% increase. University of Cambridge natural-hazards researcher Maximillian Van Wyk de Vries calls for a tiered system combining satellite screening, detailed assessments, ground monitoring and, where warranted, lake lowering. He also calls for sustained funding and local early-warning and evacuation plans.

items.title: [list.solar] Solar EV maker Aptera completes first customer-bound vehicle, delivery pending
items.content_html: Aptera Motors, a California solar-electric vehicle developer, has completed its first vehicle intended for sale to a customer, but has not delivered it. The three-wheeled car was built for Martin Hartono, chief executive of GDP Venture, and is intended for export; Aptera has not announced a delivery date or destination country. The company says body-integrated solar panels can provide up to about 40 miles of driving per day in favorable conditions. Aptera reported $9.2 million in cash on Sept. 30 and said its cash would not cover operations for the next 12 months; it estimated that starting production requires about $25 million. In October, it said it planned to begin building its first 40 production vehicles by year-end, with customer deliveries targeted for early 2027, subject to financing.

The California expansion adds about 200,000 square feet and represents an investment of more than $100 million; the planned investment in the Oak Ridge project is about $280 million. Radiant expects to begin operating its Tennessee fueling facility in 2027 and start commercial deliveries in 2028. Its first Kaleidos unit is at Idaho National Laboratory for testing, and the U.S. Department of Energy has approved its safety analysis ahead of a full-power test campaign.

items.title: [apnews.com] COP31 talks overrun as vulnerable nations seek climate finance
items.content_html: COP31 negotiations in Antalya continued past their scheduled Friday close as representatives of climate-vulnerable countries pressed for firm funding commitments to prepare for worsening climate impacts. The summit’s nearly 200 countries remained divided over a political agreement, including whether it should call for a transition away from fossil fuels. Ghana’s Zanetor Agyeman-Rawlings, who leads the African negotiating group, said public adaptation funding from developed countries totaled $28.2 billion to $31.7 billion in 2024, compared with an estimated need of about $305 billion annually by 2035. The revised draft offered no detailed commitments on the issue; a report is expected before the 2027 climate conference in Ethiopia. Pacific island representatives also pointed to a funding shortfall for climate resilience: the Pacific Resilience Facility remained about $300 million short of its $500 million goal after a summit event drew just one new offer, $5 million from Australian mining executive and philanthropist Andrew Forrest. At a late Friday plenary, delegates approved technical decisions but left the main political text unresolved. COP31 President Murat Kurum said a new draft was expected Saturday.

items.title: [deccanchronicle.com] Andhra Pradesh approves exploration of small reactors as an alternative to thermal power
items.content_html: Andhra Pradesh approved exploring the use of small modular reactors (SMRs) as an alternative to thermal power on Nov. 20, under an order issued by K Vijayanand, the state’s special chief secretary for energy. The approval followed a proposal from the Andhra Pradesh Power Generation Corporation (APGENCO). It allows the state to study the option, not build a plant. The state may consider sites of retiring thermal power plants or other suitable locations, but will consider building plants after SMR technology stabilises. The order permits private-sector participation and directs APGENCO’s managing director to take the necessary next steps.

items.title: [canarymedia.com] North Carolina regulators defer Duke solar procurement after canceling 2026 bids
items.content_html: North Carolina regulators have confirmed that Duke Energy will not solicit solar bids in 2026, shifting some planned procurement into later years. The commission’s decision approving Duke’s carbon-reduction plan calls for 2.3 gigawatts of additional solar to come online by 2034, but leaves more than a gigawatt of planned procurement unfulfilled this year. Clean-energy groups say skipping a year of bidding could lead to higher costs because tariffs and inflation may push solar prices up. Regulators cited federal tariffs and expiring tax credits as factors making solar more expensive, along with lower near-term demand after state lawmakers repealed a carbon-reduction requirement. Duke must tell the commission by Nov. 26 how it will meet its solar projections.

items.title: [energynews.biz] Data center electricity demand set to double as grid rules tighten
items.content_html: The International Energy Agency (IEA) forecasts that global data-center electricity use will nearly double to about 1,000 terawatt-hours a year by 2030, with artificial intelligence driving roughly three-quarters of the increase; associated emissions could rise about 70%. On Thursday, the U.S. Senate passed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, 62-33. The bill would require data centers to pay for grid costs and shorten approval timelines for energy infrastructure. It now goes to the House after the Thanksgiving break. The Senate measure has divided lawmakers: supporters say it could fund grid expansion and accelerate clean-energy connections, while opponents warn that faster approvals could spur gas-fired power and data-center construction. A Harvard-led study estimated that 403 U.S. hyperscale facilities used about 82 terawatt-hours of electricity annually and were linked to roughly 26 million metric tons of carbon dioxide. Oregon regulators approved rules requiring new Pacific Power data centers to cover their energy costs starting Jan. 1, 2027. Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek has also called for state oversight legislation during the session beginning Jan. 11, 2027.

items.title: [leparisien.fr] Record-strength El Niño set to peak in December, raising weather risks
items.content_html: The World Meteorological Organization says the strengthening El Niño is expected to peak in December and is almost certain to persist through February 2027, with a chance of ranking among the strongest since 1950. The agency forecasts unusually warm conditions across much of the world and shifting rainfall patterns that could increase drought and flood risks. U.S. seasonal outlooks favor above-average winter temperatures across much of the northern United States and wetter conditions with elevated coastal flooding risk in California. Unusually high tides beginning Nov. 24 could coincide with storms and heavy rain in California, though forecasters say storm timing and rainfall remain uncertain. High tides are also forecast for Dec. 23-25 and Jan. 21-22, extending the period when storm waves could push water inland.

items.title: [straitstimes.com] IEA says Iran shock speeds electrification but may prolong coal use
items.content_html: The International Energy Agency says the energy disruption linked to the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran is accelerating countries’ shift toward electrification. The agency said 25 countries had announced new electrification-related policies since February as governments seek more domestic energy sources. At the U.N. climate talks, COP31, host Türkiye is pressing to raise electricity’s share of global energy use from about 21% to 35% by 2035; draft negotiating text does not specify that the added power must come from renewables. The IEA also said buildings now use more energy for cooling than for heating, a shift it links to rising temperatures and demand for air conditioning. The agency expects solar and nuclear power to gain ground, but energy-security concerns could keep coal in use as backup, particularly in coal-rich Asian economies. It warned that inadequate electricity grids, charging infrastructure and supply capacity could slow electrification.

items.title: [hu.euronews.com] IEA warns AI data-centre boom could strain grids and raise costs
items.content_html: Electricity networks could struggle to connect a rapidly growing number of data centres, the International Energy Agency (IEA), a global energy watchdog, said in its World Energy Outlook published Nov. 19. Grid upgrades could delay projects and raise questions about who pays for new infrastructure. The IEA expects data-centre electricity use to double by 2030, with artificial intelligence driving three-quarters of the increase. It also warned that planned developments in some markets could exceed current peak power demand. In France, about 80 data-centre projects had reserved nearly 18 gigawatts of grid capacity by May 2026, while connected sites were using, on average, about one-fifth of the power they had requested. A regional study put the average cost of connecting to the transmission grid at about €30 million, with some costs covered by regulated network charges. French grid operator RTE is planning shared development zones to spread infrastructure costs among users. The IEA identified underuse, early exit and cancellation as financial risks. Regulators are seeking guarantees and minimum payments to limit losses if projects are abandoned.

items.title: [energynow.com] Venezuela uses AI to curb methane while expanding oil output
items.content_html: Venezuela is using artificial intelligence to detect methane leaks, monitor emissions and optimize oilfield operations while pursuing higher fossil-fuel production rather than a phaseout, Albania del Mar Villarroel Gomez, Venezuela’s vice minister for artificial intelligence and productive efficiency in hydrocarbons, said at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey. She said Venezuela will favor smaller, task-specific AI models over energy-intensive hyperscale systems, with computing infrastructure powered mainly by hydropower, which generates about 80% of the country’s electricity. Villarroel said the policy aims to reduce waste and emissions while maintaining energy production. Venezuela’s upstream methane-emissions intensity is nearly six times the global average, and it is the only major energy producer in Central and South America that has not signed the Global Methane Pledge.

items.title: [perthnow.com.au] Hormuz shock drives electrification, threatens gas and coal exporters
items.content_html: The International Energy Agency’s 2026 outlook says disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz is pushing governments and consumers toward domestic energy supplies, electrification and more diverse suppliers. In the IEA’s prolonged-disruption case, oil demand in 2035 could be 4.4 million barrels a day below its stated-policy scenario; electric vehicles alone would displace more than 11 million barrels a day. The IEA models Australian coal exports falling about 11% by 2035, while a potential gas glut could push prices down. The agency also says inadequate electricity grids, charging networks and power supplies could slow electrification, while higher fuel costs risk stalling recent gains in access to electricity and clean cooking in developing economies. The IEA says governments are increasingly making energy security and affordability central to policy, but its modeled pathways are scenarios, not forecasts. If the conflict reaches a clear end, delayed liquefied natural gas (LNG) supplies could reach the market and weigh on oil and gas prices even as buyers rebuild inventories.

items.title: [euronews.com] Harvard study links data-center carbon costs to local power grids
items.content_html: The climate impact of U.S. data centers depends strongly on where they draw electricity: generating the same amount of power emitted more than twice as much carbon in coal-heavy Wyoming as in Oregon, where hydropower is significant, researchers found. A Harvard University study estimated that 403 large U.S. data centers emitted 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide between May 2024 and April 2025. Harvard postdoctoral researcher Gianluca Guidi told PBS that Virginia, Iowa, Oregon and Ohio together account for half the facilities’ electricity use, and that communities hosting them may bear pollution and infrastructure costs without receiving the same benefits. The study did not assess health effects, but Guidi said additional electricity demand can mean more power plants and pollution, along with pressure on local infrastructure.

Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka said the measure lets the government mobilize resources and coordinate aid. Officials allocated 20 million Fijian dollars from existing funds for emergency water supplies for families and farmers. The declaration runs for one month and can be extended or revoked on advice from the National Disaster Risk Management Council. The Fiji Meteorological Service forecast below-normal rainfall from November through April 2027 and above-normal daytime temperatures through January across most of the country. The U.S. Climate Prediction Center put the chance of a strong-to-very-strong El Niño from January through March at more than 79%, while Australian officials said in June the event could become one of the strongest in seven decades.

items.content_html: Bangladesh’s first nuclear power reactor began supplying electricity to the national grid on Nov. 17, when Unit 1 at the Russian-built Rooppur plant was synchronized with the grid at about 40% of its rated power. Its generator produced 370 megawatts at synchronization, said Alexey Likhachev, director general of Russia’s state nuclear corporation Rosatom. Rooppur’s two reactors are designed for a combined 2,400 MW; the second unit is expected to follow in 2027.

items.title: [news.un.org] COP31 ministers face deadlock over fossil fuels, finance and science
items.content_html: Ministers at the United Nations COP31 climate summit in Antalya remained deadlocked Wednesday over a final agreement, with 21 issues unresolved and only days left before the conference’s scheduled close Friday, Nov. 20. Disputes include whether to call for a transition away from fossil fuels, how to fund climate adaptation and whether to set a global electrification goal. A draft political deal released Monday included competing proposals on fossil fuels, climate finance, the 1.5°C goal, science and trade. Turkey’s proposal to raise electricity’s share of global final energy use to 35% by 2035 has support from 75 countries, but some governments oppose including it in the final text. Countries also disagree over when the next assessments from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), the UN-backed climate science body, should be ready. Vulnerable countries want them before the 2028 global review, while others favor 2029. Ministers met informally Wednesday to seek compromises; a revised draft was expected Thursday.

items.title: [european-union.europa.eu] EU agrees to streamline permits for renewable projects and power grids
items.content_html: The Council of the European Union and the European Parliament reached a provisional agreement on Nov. 18 to speed up permitting for renewable energy projects, electricity grids and storage facilities, aiming to reduce construction delays and strengthen energy security. The changes also cover recharging stations and authorizations for new electricity and gas infrastructure. The agreement streamlines deadlines for approvals and grid connections and provides for digital portals to handle applications. Both institutions must still endorse and formally adopt it after a legal and linguistic review; member states will then have 18 months to incorporate the directive into national law.

items.title: [pv-magazine.com] Moment Energy launches certified second-life battery system for businesses

It has UL safety certifications and independent verification under U.S. foreign-entity sourcing rules, which the company says could qualify it for federal investment tax credits from 2027. Orders opened Nov. 18, 2026, with first deliveries expected in the first quarter of 2027. Nova can discharge at full power for two hours; Moment says its compact design is intended for sites including hospitals, airports and manufacturing facilities.

items.title: [theguardian.com] UK climate advisers warn weaker EV rules could add 8.4m tonnes of CO2 a year
items.content_html: The UK’s Climate Change Committee warned that loosening electric-vehicle sales rules could add 8.4 million tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions a year by the next decade and make the country likely to miss legally binding climate targets. The government is consulting on lowering the zero-emission vehicle requirement, which currently requires zero-emission vehicles to account for 80% of new car sales by 2030 and 100% by 2035. The committee says the rules account for the largest share of planned emissions cuts through 2037; weakening them would require comparable reductions elsewhere to meet the carbon budget for 2033-37. Its chair, Nigel Topping, also warned that reducing the targets would increase the UK’s exposure to volatile oil markets, while the government says the consultation will not change its stated phaseout dates for petrol and diesel vehicles.

items.title: [canarymedia.com] Google backs $500 million Oregon geothermal project for data centers
items.content_html: Google has agreed to buy 50 megawatts of power from Quaise Energy’s proposed Project Obsidian geothermal plant near Oregon’s Newberry Volcano, with deliveries to three Google data centers in The Dalles expected as early as 2030. Quaise and Google did not disclose the sale price, but Quaise valued the agreement at more than $500 million, according to Canary Media and The Wall Street Journal. The deal is the first commercial power purchase announced for a superhot-rock geothermal project. Quaise plans to use conventional drilling in the project’s first phase and introduce its experimental millimeter-wave drilling in a later phase. The technology aims to reach hotter, deeper rock, but the project remains under development, and the experimental method has not been used at commercial scale. The project will also require a new transmission line to connect the site to the grid.

items.title: [bbc.co.uk] Earthshot Prize names five climate innovators in Mumbai, awards £1 million each
items.content_html: Prince William, Prince of Wales, announced five winners of the 2026 Earthshot Prize in Mumbai on Nov. 17, awarding each £1 million ($1.3 million) to expand environmental projects. The recipients were Indian electric-vehicle maker Mahindra Last Mile Mobility, campaign group PFAS-Free France, Niue Ocean Wide Trust, offshore wind company Ørsted and Bhutan, which was recognized for forest conservation. They were selected from 15 finalists working on clean transport, pollution, marine protection, renewable energy and conservation. The awards coincided with the United Nations COP31 climate talks, where countries have struggled to agree on fossil fuels and climate finance. A U.N. report released in October said the world was on course to exceed the 1.5-degree Celsius warming threshold. William called for urgent action, saying, “They will not judge us by the promises we made, but by the world we leave behind”.

items.title: [computerbase.de] EcoFlow opens Stream 5000 storage to Home Assistant and cloud-free operation
items.content_html: Since November 17, EcoFlow has been rolling out a firmware update for the Stream 5000 and Stream AC 5000 home batteries. It adds official integration with the Home Assistant smart home platform, as well as a local mode in which the app and battery communicate over the home network without using the EcoFlow cloud. The rollout is expected to take about a week. Older Stream models initially get these features only if users operate them together with a 5000-series device. In local mode, real-time monitoring and basic controls remain available. Home Assistant can also change settings through the connection, provided users grant the relevant permission.

items.title: [rapporteur.com] France's fusion plan backs €22bn ITER, which will not generate electricity
items.content_html: France’s new fusion roadmap centers on the €22 billion International Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor (ITER) in southern France, which is designed to test fusion, not generate electricity. France aims to develop technologies for a European pilot plant by 2035. Its strategy also relies on the WEST tokamak at Cadarache and the Laser Mégajoule facility near Bordeaux. ITER’s current plan calls for deuterium-deuterium fusion operations in 2035, following years of schedule changes. Its experimental target is 500 megawatts of fusion power for at least 400 seconds, using 50 megawatts of plasma-heating power. The revised plan was announced in June 2025.
